etymology: A dialect past participle of turn (turned up → turnt up → turnt), from Southern and Atlanta hip-hop of the late 2000s, where turn up meant to get wild at a party. It spread across Twitter and Vine from about 2012; the 2013 club hit "Turn Down for What" (DJ Snake and Lil Jon) made the attitude a national chant. Turnt covers a range from hyped and energetic to thoroughly drunk or high ("turnt up," "too turnt"). Its opposite, turnt down, means calmed or sober.
biblical_def: To be turnt is to be at full party intensity: loud, wild, uninhibited, and in most usage intoxicated. "Getting turnt" is the plan for a Friday night; "too turnt" is the state in which one regrets the photos the next morning. The Christian observation: the word sometimes means only high spirits, but its centre of gravity is drunkenness, and Scripture names that plainly. "And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit" (Eph 5:18). "Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise" (Pro 20:1). The prophets pronounced woe on the culture of the all-night party: "Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!" (Isa 5:11). Peter told new believers that the old life of "excess of wine, revellings, banquetings" had lasted long enough (1Pe 4:3). The deeper point is in Ephesians: the turnt state is a counterfeit filling. Men drink to be lifted out of themselves, freed from fear, loosened into joy. The Spirit gives the real thing, and it leaves a man more himself, not less. A father tells his son: you will be offered a night of being turnt in exchange for your judgment; it is a bad trade every time. Learn to have a great time sober, and you will remember your best nights.
webster_summary: Millennial hip-hop slang (late 2000s; mainstream 2012–2014) for party-wild, usually intoxicated; Scripture calls it drunkenness and offers the true filling: be not drunk with wine, but be filled with the Spirit (Eph 5:18). Reject.
webster_full: TURNT, adj. (Millennial slang, late 2000s–2010s; dialect past participle of turn up) Wildly excited; partying hard; often drunk or high. "We got turnt." Also turnt up; opposite turnt down.

Webster (1828), root turn: TURN, verb transitive [Latin turnus; torniare, to turn; tornare, to return; torneare, tornire, to turn to fence round, to tilt; torniamento, tournament.] 1. To cause to move in a circular course; as, to turn a wheel; to turn a spindle; to turn the body. 2. To change or shift sides; to put the upper side downwards, or one side in the place of the other. It is said a hen turns her eggs often when sitting. 3. To alter, as a position. Expert When to advance, or stand, or turn the sway of battle. 4. To cause to preponderate; […]
Decode for parents: "getting turnt" almost always means drinking; ask the plain question.
scriptures: Eph 5:18
And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit;
Pro 20:1
Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise.
Isa 5:11
Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!
For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries:
Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it moveth itself aright. At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder.
corruption_summary: Turnt makes intoxication the goal of a good night; Scripture calls it excess and offers the Spirit’s filling, which brings joy without the loss of self.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is that the word makes the loss of control the point. A party is judged by how turnt it got; the stories told afterward are about who lost the most judgment. Proverbs describes the progression with uncomfortable precision: "Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it moveth itself aright. At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder" (Pro 23:31-32). The night that begins as fun ends with someone in a ditch, in a bed they regret, or in a cell.

The recovery is not a joyless refusal but a better fullness. Paul sets drunkenness and the Spirit side by side because both promise to lift a man beyond himself; only one keeps the promise. The Spirit-filled life overflows in "speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord" (Eph 5:19), and the joy is still there in the morning. Teach the young that sobriety is not boredom, that the best celebrations in Scripture were feasts before the Lord, and that a clear head is a gift to their future selves.
roots_summary: Old English turnian (Latin tornare, to turn on a lathe) → turn up → Southern hip-hop turnt (up) → 2013 "Turn Down for What."
roots_lines: Latin tornare — to turn on a lathe; Old English turnian
Late 2000s: Southern / Atlanta hip-hop turn up, turnt up
2012–2014: Twitter and Vine spread turnt; 2013 "Turn Down for What"
Opposite: turnt down — calm, sober
Biblical anchor: be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit (Eph 5:18)
usage: "Party at Jake’s. We’re getting turnt."
Wine is a mocker (Pro 20:1); the Spirit is the better filling (Eph 5:18).
The time past may suffice for excess of wine and revellings (1Pe 4:3).

etymology: From the ordinary phrasal verb turn up (to increase, as the volume), re-coined in late-2000s Southern hip-hop and club culture to mean to party with maximum energy, or to get someone else hyped. As a noun, a turn-up is a wild party or an energetic moment. Lil Jon’s 2000s crunk records set the tone; the 2013 single "Turn Down for What" (DJ Snake and Lil Jon) made the phrase a chant. By the mid-2010s, "turn up" could mean celebration of any kind, including at sports games and graduations.
biblical_def: To turn up is to raise the energy of a gathering: to party hard, to celebrate loudly, to get everyone hyped. Unlike its cousin turnt, the phrase does not always imply drinking; a team can turn up after a win, and a family can turn up at a wedding. The Christian observation: Scripture is not against turning up. It commands feasting. Israel’s calendar was full of celebrations where God told His people to rejoice before Him with food and music. When the prodigal came home, the father said, "bring hither the fatted calf, and kill it; and let us eat, and be merry" (Luk 15:23). David "danced before the LORD with all his might" (2Sa 6:14). And Nehemiah told a weeping crowd, "Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet … for the joy of the LORD is your strength" (Neh 8:10). The question is not whether to celebrate but before Whom and how. Paul draws the line: "Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness" (Rom 13:13). The Preacher, who tried every kind of party, concluded of mirth, "What doeth it?" (Ecc 2:2) when it is pursued for itself. A father teaches his children to turn up at weddings, birthdays, and Easter, loud and glad, and to avoid the kind of party where the celebration is just the excuse.
webster_summary: Millennial hip-hop slang (late 2000s; 2013 "Turn Down for What") for partying or celebrating with maximum energy; Scripture commands joyful feasting before the Lord (Luk 15:23) and forbids rioting and drunkenness (Rom 13:13).
webster_full: TURN UP, v.i. / n. (Millennial slang, late 2000s–2010s) To party or celebrate with high energy; to hype a crowd. "Time to turn up." A turn-up: a wild party. Related: turnt, "Turn Down for What."

Webster (1828), root turn: TURN, verb transitive [Latin turnus; torniare, to turn; tornare, to return; torneare, tornire, to turn to fence round, to tilt; torniamento, tournament.] 1. To cause to move in a circular course; as, to turn a wheel; to turn a spindle; to turn the body. 2. To change or shift sides; to put the upper side downwards, or one side in the place of the other. It is said a hen turns her eggs often when sitting. 3. To alter, as a position. Expert When to advance, or stand, or turn the sway of battle. 4. To cause to preponderate; […]
Decode for parents: "turning up" can mean innocent celebration or a drinking party; ask where, with whom, and who is in charge.
scriptures: And bring hither the fatted calf, and kill it; and let us eat, and be merry:
And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod.
Neh 8:10

Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength.
Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying.
Ecc 2:2
I said of laughter, It is mad: and of mirth, What doeth it?
corruption_summary: Turn up can name holy celebration or a riot; Scripture commands feasting before the Lord and forbids the party that is only an excuse for excess.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is celebration cut loose from anything to celebrate. The Millennial turn-up often has no occasion but the weekend, and its energy has to be supplied chemically or by escalation, because there is no real joy at the centre. Solomon tried that experiment with all his resources and reported the result: "I said of laughter, It is mad: and of mirth, What doeth it?" (Ecc 2:2). Rioting is what celebration becomes when it has nothing to rejoice in.

The recovery is the feast with a reason. The Church’s calendar, its weddings, its baptisms, and its Lord’s Days are occasions for real joy, and Christians should throw the best parties in town: loud singing, long tables, dancing at weddings, children up late. Teach the young that the opposite of a drunken turn-up is not a quiet room but a feast where the Lord is honoured and everyone goes home glad and clear-headed.
roots_summary: Turn + up (increase the volume) → late-2000s crunk and Southern hip-hop turn up → 2013 "Turn Down for What" → general celebration slang.
roots_lines: Latin tornare → Old English turnian + up
Late 2000s: crunk and Southern hip-hop turn up — to party hard
2013: DJ Snake and Lil Jon, "Turn Down for What"
Mid-2010s: generalized to any high-energy celebration
Biblical anchor: let us eat, and be merry (Luk 15:23); not in rioting and drunkenness (Rom 13:13)
usage: "We won state! Turn up!"
Turn up at the prodigal’s homecoming (Luk 15:23), not at the riot (Rom 13:13).
The joy of the LORD is your strength (Neh 8:10).

etymology: Military English since the 1640s, from French escouade, Spanish escuadra, Italian squadra (a square of soldiers), from Latin ex + quadrare. In 2010s slang, especially from 2014–2015, squad meant one’s close group of friends, often stylish and loyal ("my squad," "squad up"). Taylor Swift’s celebrity "girl squad" and the Bad Blood video (2015) made it a cultural event; the hashtag #squadgoals followed, and "squad" became shorthand for any tight crew.
biblical_def: Your squad is your crew: the handful of friends you show up with, stand up for, and do life beside. The word borrows the military sense of a small unit that fights together, and that borrowing is apt. The Christian observation: the thing named is good and biblical. Men and women were not made to go through life alone, and God’s work has often been done by small bands. Jonathan’s armourbearer told him, "Do all that is in thine heart: turn thee; behold, I am with thee according to thy heart" (1Sa 14:7), and the two of them routed a garrison. David’s mighty men are named one by one (2Sa 23:8). The Lord Jesus chose twelve "that they should be with him" (Mar 3:14), and within them an inner three. "And if one prevail against him, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken" (Ecc 4:12). The question every squad must answer is the one Proverbs asks: "He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed" (Pro 13:20). A squad shapes a young person more than almost anything else; it will make him braver or make him worse. A father asks his son and daughter about their squads, not to control them but to help them choose friends who will stand with them in the right fight, and he prays that each child will have at least a few who would follow them into battle for the Lord.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (2014–2015, from the military unit) for one’s close crew of friends; redeemable, for God works through small faithful bands (1Sa 14:7; Ecc 4:12), and a squad must be chosen wisely (Pro 13:20).
webster_full: SQUAD, n. (Millennial slang, c. 2014–present; from the military unit) One’s close group of friends. "Me and the squad." Also squad up, #squadgoals, girl squad.
Webster (1828), root squad: SQUAD, noun A company of armed men; a party learning military exercise; any small party.
Decode for parents: know your child’s squad by name; it is the strongest influence after home.
scriptures: And his armourbearer said unto him, Do all that is in thine heart: turn thee; behold, I am with thee according to thy heart.
Mar 3:14
And he ordained twelve, that they should be with him, and that he might send them forth to preach,
Ecc 4:12
And if one prevail against him, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.
And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works:
corruption_summary: Squad names good companionship, but can become an exclusive clique or a crew that dares its members into folly; Scripture’s band is chosen for wisdom and gathered for the Lord’s work.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift is toward the clique: the squad as an exclusive, curated image, defined by who is kept out and by the photos it posts. Celebrity "squads" made friendship a brand. And a squad can be a pressure system that pushes its members toward the dumbest thing anyone dares. Proverbs warns the son against exactly that crew: "Cast in thy lot among us; let us all have one purse: My son, walk not thou in the way with them" (Pro 1:14-15).

The recovery is the band with a mission. "And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works" (Heb 10:24). A Christian squad goads its members toward courage, purity, and service; it prays together, rebukes one another gently, and includes the lonely. Teach the young to choose friends like Jonathan’s armourbearer: loyal, brave, and pointed toward God’s battle, not their own glory.
roots_summary: Latin ex + quadrare (to square) → Italian squadra, French escouade → English squad (1640s, military) → 2014–2015 friend-group slang.
roots_lines: Latin quadrare — to make square; Italian squadra — a square of soldiers
1640s: English squad, a small military unit
2014–2015: squad = close friend group; Taylor Swift’s "girl squad"
2015: #squadgoals; squad up
Biblical anchor: I am with thee according to thy heart (1Sa 14:7); a threefold cord (Ecc 4:12)
usage: "The squad’s coming over after the game."
A threefold cord is not quickly broken (Ecc 4:12): choose it well.
A companion of fools shall be destroyed (Pro 13:20).

etymology: From goal (Middle English gol, a boundary or limit). In 2013–2015 social media, goals or #goals became a one-word caption for anything aspirational: a couple’s photo ("relationship goals"), a friend group ("squad goals"), a body, a kitchen, a vacation. The usage spread through Twitter and Instagram, where tagging an image goals marked it as a model life to aim for. Gen Z later shifted to "it’s giving" and other forms, but goals remains common.
biblical_def: Goals is the one-word caption for aspiration: a photo of a couple on a beach is "relationship goals," a sculpted torso is "body goals," a white kitchen is "house goals." The word turns other people’s curated moments into targets for one’s own life. The Christian observation: aiming is good, and Scripture gives believers a goal. "I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus" (Php 3:14). "Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain" (1Co 9:24). But the #goals habit has three hidden problems. First, it sets its targets by images, and images lie; the couple was arguing ten minutes before the photo. Second, it cultivates the old sin of coveting by scroll: "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s house … nor any thing that is thy neighbour’s" (Exo 20:17). Third, it makes the visible life the aim, when Scripture tells us to "Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth" (Col 3:2). A father asks his children: whose life are you aiming at, and do you know what it costs? Then he gives them better targets: faithfulness, wisdom, a godly marriage built over decades, a body kept as a temple and not an idol. "Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established" (Pro 16:3).
webster_summary: Millennial social-media slang (2013–2015, #goals) marking a curated image as a life to aim at; Scripture gives the true mark (Php 3:14) and warns against coveting by scroll (Exo 20:17).
webster_full: GOALS, interj. / n. (Millennial social-media slang, 2013–present; often #goals) Said of something one aspires to. Compounds: relationship goals, squad goals, body goals, life goals.

Webster (1828), root goal: GOAL, noun 1. The point set to bound a race, and to which they run; the mark. Part curb their fiery steeds, or shun the goal With rapid wheels. 2. Any starting post. 3. The end or final purpose; the end to which a design tends, or which a person aims to reach or accomplish. Each individual seeks a several goal
Decode for parents: ask what your children are captioning as goals; that is the life they are aiming at.
scriptures: Php 3:14
I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain.
Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour's.
Col 3:2
Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth.
Pro 16:3
Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established.
corruption_summary: Goals sets life’s targets by curated images and breeds coveting by scroll; Scripture keeps the aiming and names the true mark: the high calling of God in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is aspiration by comparison. The feed shows the highlight reel of other people’s lives, and #goals converts it into a standard one’s own life fails to meet. Envy follows, then discontent with a real marriage, a real body, a real house, all of which compare badly with a photograph. The tenth commandment is a commandment against exactly this restless wanting of what belongs to another, and the scroll multiplies the neighbours whose things we can covet.

The recovery keeps the forward lean and changes the target. Paul’s goal was not a picture of a life but a Person: "That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection" (Php 3:10). Teach the young to set real goals, to work for them diligently, and to measure them by God’s Word rather than by anyone’s photos. The couple worth calling goals is the old pair in the third pew who have kept their vows for fifty years, and they never posted a thing.
roots_summary: Middle English gol (boundary, limit) → goal (end of a race; object of ambition) → 2013–2015 caption #goals, relationship goals.
roots_lines: Middle English gol — a boundary, a limit
16th c.: goal — the end point of a race; then the object of an effort
2013–2015: #goals, relationship goals, squad goals on Twitter and Instagram
Visual aspiration culture: the curated image as target
Biblical anchor: I press toward the mark (Php 3:14); thou shalt not covet (Exo 20:17)
usage: "Matching outfits at the airport? Relationship goals."
The mark worth pressing toward is the high calling of God in Christ (Php 3:14).
Set your affection on things above (Col 3:2).

etymology: An extendable pole for holding a camera or phone at arm’s-plus length to take a self-portrait. A 1983 Japanese patent by Hiroshi Ueda and Yujiro Mima of Minolta described an "extender" for compact cameras; Wayne Fromm’s Quik Pod (2005) refined it. The name selfie stick followed selfie (Oxford Dictionaries Word of the Year, 2013), and in 2014 the device was everywhere: Time named it one of the year’s best inventions. In 2015 Disney parks, many museums, and stadiums banned it for safety and courtesy.
biblical_def: A selfie stick is a pole that lets a person photograph himself from further away, getting the landmark, the crowd, or the friends into the frame with him at the centre. The device was briefly the emblem of the Millennial tourist: at the Colosseum, the Grand Canyon, the Sistine Chapel, a forest of poles pointed back at their owners. The Christian observation: a gadget is not a sin, and a group photo on a family trip is a good memory. But the selfie stick is a striking picture of a posture of soul. It literally extends a person’s reach so that he can turn his back on the wonder and put himself in front of it. Paul foresaw an age when "men shall be lovers of their own selves" (2Ti 3:2), and the cure he preached was a different orientation: "Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others" (Php 2:4). John the Baptist, seeing Jesus, said the sentence that is the opposite of the selfie stick: "He must increase, but I must decrease" (Joh 3:30). The Psalmist turns the camera away: "Not unto us, O LORD, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory" (Psa 115:1). A father on vacation takes his pictures and then puts the phone away and makes his children look: at the canyon, the cathedral, the ocean, and the God who made the eye that sees them.
webster_summary: Millennial-era gadget (patent 1983; craze 2014; banned at many venues 2015) for extended self-portraits; harmless as a tool, an emblem of the self put in front of every wonder (2Ti 3:2; Joh 3:30).
webster_full: SELFIE STICK, n. (Millennial slang and product, 2014–present) An extendable handheld pole holding a phone or camera for self-portraits. Banned from many theme parks, museums, and stadiums (2015).

Webster (1828), root stick: STICK, noun [G. This word is connected with the verb to stick with stock, stack, and other words having the like elements. The primary sense of the root is to thrust, to shoot, and to set.] 1. The small shoot or branch of a tree or shrub, cut off; a rod; also, a staff; as, to strike one with a stick 2. Any stem of a tree, of any size, cut for fuel or timber. It is applied in America to any long and slender piece of timber, round or square, from the smallest size to the largest, used in the frames of buildings; […]
Decode for parents: on your next trip, count how many photos face the wonder and how many face your children; then turn some around.
scriptures: For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy,
Php 2:4
Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others.
Joh 3:30
He must increase, but I must decrease.
Not unto us, O LORD, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory, for thy mercy, and for thy truth's sake.
When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?
corruption_summary: The selfie stick extends the self in front of every wonder; harmless as a tool, it pictures the age of lovers of their own selves, which the Baptist answers: He must increase.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is not the pole but the reflex it serves: experience as a backdrop for self-documentation. At the great sights of the world, crowds now stand with their backs to the thing they travelled to see, arranging themselves in front of it. The habit trains attention inward. Even worship is now photographed from the pew. The love of self that Paul lists first among the marks of the last days needs no stick, but it was never more conveniently equipped.

The recovery is wonder that forgets itself. "When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" (Psa 8:3-4). That is the posture of a man looking outward and upward, and it makes the self smaller and happier. Teach children to look long at what they came to see, to photograph it if they like, and to stand in front of it less often than they stand in awe of it.
roots_summary: Old English sticca (stick) + selfie (2002, Australian; Oxford WOTY 2013) → 1983 Minolta "extender" patent → 2005 Quik Pod → 2014 craze → 2015 bans.
roots_lines: Old English sticca — a stick, a rod
1983: Ueda and Mima, Minolta, patent a camera "extender"
2005: Wayne Fromm’s Quik Pod; 2013: selfie named Word of the Year
2014: selfie stick craze; 2015: venue bans
Biblical anchor: men shall be lovers of their own selves (2Ti 3:2); He must increase (Joh 3:30)
usage: "Hold the selfie stick higher so we get the waterfall."
Turn the camera to the wonder: not unto us, O LORD (Psa 115:1).
He must increase, but I must decrease (Joh 3:30).

etymology: The pursed-lip, sucked-in-cheek pose of 2000s self-portraits, named for its resemblance to a duck’s bill. It flourished in the MySpace and early Facebook era (roughly 2005–2012) and was mocked by name from about 2007 (blogs and the site duckfaceblog catalogued it). The pose aimed to make lips fuller and cheekbones sharper. Online dictionaries admitted duck face by 2014; by the late 2010s it was a Millennial cliché that Gen Z ridiculed.
biblical_def: Duck face is the pout: lips pushed forward, cheeks pulled in, eyes up at the camera. It was the signature selfie pose of Millennial girls (and not a few boys) in the MySpace years, meant to look alluring and ended up looking like a mallard. The Christian observation: the pose is a small, almost comic thing, and it opens on a real question about what a girl is learning to do with her face. Duck face was a practised, rehearsed expression made for an audience: a way of offering the face as an object of desire. Scripture has a sharp portrait of that posture: the daughters of Zion who "walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go" (Isa 3:16). It also has a better word for a woman’s face. Peter calls women away from adornment that is merely outward, and toward "the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price" (1Pe 3:4). Paul asks for "shamefacedness and sobriety" (1Ti 2:9), an old word for a face that is not trying to provoke. And every girl’s actual face is a gift: "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made" (Psa 139:14). A father tells his daughter: you do not need to make faces at a camera to be lovely; the face God gave you, smiling at people you love, is the one worth photographing.
webster_summary: Millennial selfie slang (2000s MySpace era) for the pursed-lip pout; a small rehearsed seduction for an audience, which Scripture contrasts with shamefacedness and the meek and quiet spirit (1Ti 2:9; 1Pe 3:4).
webster_full: DUCK FACE, n. (Millennial slang, c. 2005–2015) The pouting selfie expression with lips pushed out and cheeks sucked in. Also duckface; succeeded by the "fish gape" and other poses.

Webster (1828), root duck: DUCK, noun [from the verb, to duck ] 1. A water fowl, so called from its plunging. There are many species or varieties of the duck some wild, others tame. 2. An inclination of the head, resembling the motion of a duck in water. 3. A stone thrown obliquely on the water so as to rebound; as in duck and drake.
Decode for parents: notice what your daughter is learning to do with her face for a camera, and tell her what you see when she laughs.
scriptures: Isa 3:16
Moreover the LORD saith, Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet:
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;
I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.
Pro 6:25
Lust not after her beauty in thine heart; neither let her take thee with her eyelids.
corruption_summary: Duck face rehearses the face as an object of display; Scripture prefers shamefacedness, the meek and quiet spirit, and the face God gave.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is small and formative: girls learning to manufacture an expression for strangers. Practised in front of a phone a thousand times, the pose teaches that one’s face is a product to be optimized for attention. Proverbs warns a young man about the woman who uses her face as a lure, "neither let her take thee with her eyelids" (Pro 6:25); the duck face is a clumsy, adolescent version of the same art, and it trains both the girl who makes it and the boys who rate it.

The recovery is the unrehearsed face. The best photographs of a family are the ones where nobody was posing: a child laughing, a grandmother’s look, a bride seeing her father. Teach daughters that their faces were made for joy, kindness, and worship rather than for performance, and teach sons to honour a girl’s face by looking her in the eye rather than evaluating a pose.
roots_summary: Old English duce (duck, "diver") → 2000s MySpace pout → c. 2007 mocking label duck face → 2014 online dictionaries → late-2010s Millennial cliché.
roots_lines: Old English duce — the duck, literally "diver," from ducan, to dive
c. 2005–2012: the pursed-lip selfie of MySpace and early Facebook
c. 2007: duck face named and mocked on blogs
2014: in online dictionaries; late 2010s: Gen Z mockery
Biblical anchor: shamefacedness and sobriety (1Ti 2:9); a meek and quiet spirit (1Pe 3:4)
usage: "Every picture from 2009 is duck face."
The face worth photographing is laughing, not posing (Psa 139:14).
The ornament of a meek and quiet spirit is of great price (1Pe 3:4).

etymology: A compound of photo and bomb (in the sense of to spoil, as in a joke that "bombs"), for intruding into someone else’s photograph at the moment it is taken, usually with a silly face or gesture. Used online from about 2008, it spread with smartphone cameras and was admitted to major dictionaries in 2014. Famous examples: Benedict Cumberbatch leaping behind U2 at the 2014 Academy Awards, and Queen Elizabeth II smiling into the background of two hockey players’ selfie at the 2014 Commonwealth Games.
biblical_def: To photobomb is to jump into another person’s picture uninvited, at the last second, usually pulling a face. Done well, it is pure comedy: the famous actor clowning behind a rock band, the queen grinning behind two athletes. Done poorly, it ruins a moment someone cared about. The Christian observation: this is a small matter of manners, and Scripture is surprisingly rich on manners. There is a time for play; laughter is good, and "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine" (Pro 17:22). The best photobombs are a gift to everyone, including the people in the picture. But Scripture also teaches the art of noticing when a joke is not wanted. "Withdraw thy foot from thy neighbour’s house; lest he be weary of thee, and so hate thee" (Pro 25:17). "He that passeth by, and meddleth with strife belonging not to him, is like one that taketh a dog by the ears" (Pro 26:17). And the general rule is plain: "study to be quiet, and to do your own business" (1Th 4:11). The bride’s portrait, the grieving family’s last photo with grandpa, the girl’s graduation picture: these are not stages for anyone’s comedy. Love rejoices with them that rejoice and weeps with them that weep, and it reads the room first. A father teaches his son that being funny is good, and knowing when not to be is better.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (c. 2008; dictionaries 2014) for jumping into another’s photo uninvited; harmless comedy when welcome, rudeness when it spoils a moment that belongs to someone else (Pro 25:17; 1Th 4:11).
webster_full: PHOTOBOMB, v.t. / n. (Millennial slang, c. 2008–present) To appear unexpectedly in another person’s photograph as it is taken, typically as a prank; the resulting picture. Also photobomber.

Webster (1828), root bomb: BOMB, [Latin bombus.] A great noise. 1. A large shell of cast iron, round and hollow, with a vent to receive a fusee, which is made of wood. This being filled with gunpowder and the fusee driven into the vent, the fusee is set on fire and the bomb is thrown from a mortar, in such a direction as to fall into a fort, city or enemy’s camp, when it bursts with great violence and often with terrible effect. The inventor of bombs is not known; they came into common use about the year 1634. 2. The stroke upon a bell.
Decode for parents: teach your jokester to read the room before he jumps into the frame.
scriptures: A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.
Withdraw thy foot from thy neighbour's house; lest he be weary of thee, and so hate thee.
He that passeth by, and meddleth with strife belonging not to him, is like one that taketh a dog by the ears.
And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you;
Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.
corruption_summary: Photobombing is play; its only fault is the prank that spoils a moment belonging to someone else, which Scripture answers with the courtesy of love.
corruption_paragraphs: The small corruption in the photobomb is self-insertion: making someone else’s moment about one’s own joke. It is the same impulse as the loud guest who turns every conversation to himself. In a culture where everything is recorded, the urge to be in every frame grows, and the prank becomes a bid for attention rather than a shared laugh.

The recovery is love that reads the room. "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep" (Rom 12:15). Sometimes the most loving thing at a celebration is to make everyone laugh; sometimes it is to stand quietly out of the frame. Teach the family clown that his gift is real and that it serves best under the rule of kindness, so that people are glad, not sorry, to see him in the picture.
roots_lines: Greek phōs — light; photograph (1839)
Greek bombos — a booming sound; bomb; slang "to bomb" — to fail, to spoil
c. 2008: photobomb online; spreads with smartphone cameras
2014: dictionaries admit it; Cumberbatch at the Oscars; the Queen at Glasgow
Biblical anchor: withdraw thy foot from thy neighbour’s house (Pro 25:17); do your own business (1Th 4:11)
usage: "Grandpa photobombed the prom pictures with bunny ears."
A merry heart doeth good like a medicine (Pro 17:22): if the room is laughing.
Weep with them that weep (Rom 12:15): stay out of that frame.

etymology: A jocular image, probably from late-2000s American campus slang, for a period of difficulty: one "rides the struggle bus" after a bad night’s sleep, a hard exam, or a rough week. It spread on Tumblr and Twitter in the early 2010s alongside "the struggle is real" (a phrase from hip-hop culture, popularized online about 2012–2013). The image is of an old, slow, crowded bus that everyone ends up on sooner or later. Also "on the struggle bus," "driving the struggle bus."
biblical_def: To be on the struggle bus is to be having a hard time and to admit it with a laugh: behind on work, exhausted, failing at adulthood for the week. The phrase is self-deprecating; it lets a person confess weakness without drama. The Christian observation: there is real wisdom in the joke. It is honest about difficulty, and it assumes, rightly, that everyone rides the bus at some point. Scripture does not pretend the Christian life is easy. Paul describes his own struggle bus: "We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed" (2Co 4:8-9). The Psalmist talks to his own soul on a hard day: "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope thou in God" (Psa 42:11). And the gospel offers a seat beside a different Passenger: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mat 11:28). The phrase also implies company, and that is biblical too: "Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ" (Gal 6:2). A father tells his children: it is no shame to say you are on the struggle bus; tell us, tell the Lord, and let us ride it with you. The shame would be suffering alone because you were too proud to admit it.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (late 2000s campus; 2010s Tumblr and Twitter) for going through a hard stretch; a redeemable honesty about weakness that Scripture meets with burden-bearing and rest in Christ (Gal 6:2; Mat 11:28).
webster_full: STRUGGLE BUS, n. (Millennial slang, late 2000s–present) A figurative vehicle carrying those having a hard time. "Riding the struggle bus this week." Related: "the struggle is real."

Webster (1828), root struggle: STRUGGLE, verb intransitive [This word may be formed on the root of stretch, right, etc. which signifies to strain; or more directly on the same elements in Latin , to wrinkle.] 1. Properly, to strive, or to make efforts with a twisting or with contortions of the body. Hence, 2. To use great efforts; to labor hard; to strive; to contend; as, to struggle to save life; to struggle with the waves; to struggle against the stream; to struggle with adversity. 3. To labor in pain or anguish; to be in agony; […]
Decode for parents: when your child jokes that she is on the struggle bus, she is telling you something true; ask what is heavy.
scriptures: We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed;
Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
Gal 6:2
Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.
corruption_summary: Struggle bus honestly admits weakness with a smile; its only risk is making a joke of a burden that needs real help, and Scripture answers with company and rest.
corruption_paragraphs: If there is a drift here, it is the joke that stops at the joke. A culture that can only admit weakness ironically may never get to the conversation where help is offered; "I’m on the struggle bus lol" can be the closest a young person comes to saying "I am not okay." Parents and pastors should hear it for what it often is: a quiet flare.

The redemption is that the struggle bus is a crowded vehicle with a good Driver. "Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you" (1Pe 5:7). The Church is meant to be the place where people say they are struggling and others sit down next to them. Teach the young to admit hardship plainly, to ask for prayer without embarrassment, and to watch for friends who are riding the bus alone.
roots_summary: Old French estroguler / Middle English struglen (struggle) + bus (from omnibus, "for all") → late-2000s campus slang → 2010s Tumblr and Twitter.
roots_lines: Middle English struglen — to contend, to strive with effort
Latin omnibus — "for all" → bus: the vehicle everyone rides
Late 2000s: campus slang "riding the struggle bus"
Early 2010s: Tumblr and Twitter; "the struggle is real"
Biblical anchor: troubled on every side, yet not distressed (2Co 4:8); bear ye one another’s burdens (Gal 6:2)
usage: "Three hours of sleep and a chem test. Total struggle bus."
Cast down, but not destroyed (2Co 4:9).
Bear ye one another’s burdens (Gal 6:2): sit next to someone on the bus.

etymology: In nineteenth-century American English a hot mess was literally a warm meal (a mess is a portion of food, as in a military mess hall). By the twentieth century it meant a difficult situation, and from the early 2000s it became Millennial slang for a person, usually a young woman, who is visibly disorganized, emotionally chaotic, or dishevelled, yet somehow endearing: the celebrity stumbling out of a club, the friend who lost her keys again. The phrase was a reality-television staple and, by the 2010s, a self-description worn with pride ("I’m a hot mess").
biblical_def: A hot mess is a person whose life is visibly falling apart in an entertaining way: late, frazzled, dramatic, chaotic, and still somehow charming. Millennial women in particular adopted it as a self-label, partly confession and partly brand. The Christian observation: the honesty is good; nobody should pretend to have it all together. But the phrase quietly turns disorder into a personality, and Scripture does not admire chaos. "For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace" (1Co 14:33). Paul tells the Church, "Let all things be done decently and in order" (1Co 14:40). The man without self-government is pictured as a ruined town: "He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls" (Pro 25:28). The old word mess also has a lovely biblical use: when Joseph fed his brothers, "he took and sent messes unto them from before him: but Benjamin’s mess was five times so much as any of theirs" (Gen 43:34). A mess was a portion from a generous table, and that is a picture of grace. The hot mess does not need to brand her chaos or despair of it; she needs the portion the Lord sends from His table, and then the slow, Spirit-given work of order. "If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature" (2Co 5:17). A father tells his daughter: you do not have to be a hot mess, and you do not have to pretend you are not one; bring the mess to Christ, and let Him set your life in order.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (2000s; once a literal warm meal) for a chaotic, frazzled, yet endearing person; honest as confession, unwise as a brand, since God is not the author of confusion but of peace (1Co 14:33).
webster_full: HOT MESS, n. (Millennial slang, 2000s–present) A person or situation in visible disarray, often endearingly so. "I’m a hot mess today." Also hot-mess express.
Older sense (19th-c. US): a hot meal; then any troublesome situation.

Webster (1828), root mess: MESS, noun [Latin mensa.] 1. A dish or a quantity of food prepared or set on a table at one time; as a mess of pottage; a mess of herbs; a mess of broth. 2. A medley; a mixed mass; a quantity. 3. As much provender or grain as is given to a beast at once. 4. A number of persons who eat together; among seamen and soldiers.
Decode for parents: when chaos becomes a personality, a child stops expecting to grow; affirm the honesty and coach the order.
scriptures: For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls.
And he took and sent messes unto them from before him: but Benjamin's mess was five times so much as any of theirs. And they drank, and were merry with him.
Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.
corruption_summary: Hot mess turns disorder into a charming identity; Scripture honours the confession, rejects chaos as a brand, and offers grace that brings order.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the brand. When "hot mess" becomes who one is, the disorder is no longer a problem to be solved but a persona to be maintained, and the persona often covers real sin: undisciplined habits, emotional excess, the trail of broken commitments. Scripture’s picture of the ungoverned life is not cute; it is a city without walls, open to every enemy.

The recovery is grace that does not leave us as we are. The gospel receives the hot mess as she is, the way Joseph fed brothers who did not deserve it, and then it begins to build walls. Self-control is a fruit of the Spirit, not a personality type. Teach the young to laugh at their chaos honestly, to bring it to the Lord, and to accept the slow help of routines, mentors, and discipline, which are how He usually builds order into a life.
roots_summary: Old French mes (a dish, a course) → mess (portion of food) → 19th-c. US hot mess (warm meal) → 20th-c. troublesome situation → 2000s chaotic person.
roots_lines: Latin missum (thing put, sent) → Old French mes — a portion of food
KJV: "Benjamin’s mess was five times so much" (Gen 43:34)
19th-c. America: hot mess — a warm meal; later, a jam
2000s: Millennial slang for a chaotic, endearing person; reality-TV staple
Biblical anchor: God is not the author of confusion, but of peace (1Co 14:33)
usage: "Spilled coffee, missed the bus, forgot my laptop. Hot mess."
Let all things be done decently and in order (1Co 14:40).
Bring the mess to the table; Joseph sent messes to brothers who did not deserve them (Gen 43:34).

etymology: From Dumpster, originally a trademark of the Dempster Brothers company of Knoxville, Tennessee (the "Dempster Dumpster," 1930s), for a large steel waste container. A literal dumpster fire is smoky, smelly, and hard to put out. The figurative sense, an utterly chaotic, disastrous situation, appears in the 2000s and became ubiquitous in 2016 commentary; the American Dialect Society chose dumpster fire as its 2016 Word of the Year. Intensified forms: tire fire, train wreck.
biblical_def: A dumpster fire is a total disaster: a project, a season, an election, or a game so badly run that it smoulders, stinks, and resists every attempt to put it out. The phrase is a Millennial shrug at chaos, half despair and half dark comedy. The Christian observation: the image is more biblical than its users know. Jerusalem had a dumpster fire. The valley of Hinnom outside the walls, once the site of child sacrifice to Molech (Jer 7:31), became in Jewish tradition the city’s burning refuse heap, and its name, Gehenna, is the word Jesus used for hell, "Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched" (Mar 9:44). The ultimate dumpster fire is not a bad week but final judgment, and the Lord spoke of it plainly so that no one would end there. Scripture also knows how small sparks start big fires: "Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!" (Jas 3:5), of the tongue. And it knows the rescue: the Lord says of a sinner snatched from judgment, "is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?" (Zec 3:2). He gives "beauty for ashes" (Isa 61:3). A father lets his children call a bad situation a dumpster fire, and then teaches them two things: that the Lord can pull a brand out of any fire, and that there is one fire no one should joke about.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (2000s; American Dialect Society Word of the Year 2016) for an utterly chaotic disaster; a harmless figure whose image recalls Gehenna, Jerusalem’s burning valley (Mar 9:44), and the brand plucked from the fire (Zec 3:2).
webster_full: DUMPSTER FIRE, n. (Millennial slang, 2000s–present; ADS Word of the Year 2016) An utterly chaotic, mismanaged, disastrous situation. "That meeting was a dumpster fire." Related: tire fire, train wreck.

Webster (1828), root fire: FIRE, noun [The radical sense of fire is usually, to rush, to rage, to be violently agitated; and if this is the sense of fire in coincides with Latin furo. It may be from shining or consuming.] 1. Heat and light emanating visibly, perceptibly and simultaneously from any body; caloric; the unknown cause of the sensation of heat and of the retrocession of the homogeneous particles of bodies from one another, producing expansion, and thus enlarging all their dimensions; one of the causes of magnetism, as evinced by Dr. […]
Decode for parents: a useful word for a bad day; a door to talk about the one fire Jesus warned about.
scriptures: Jer 7:31

And they have built the high places of Tophet, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire; which I commanded them not, neither came it into my heart.
Mar 9:44
Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched.
Jas 3:5
Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!
Zec 3:2
And the LORD said unto Satan, The LORD rebuke thee, O Satan; even the LORD that hath chosen Jerusalem rebuke thee: is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?
Isa 61:3

To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that he might be glorified.
corruption_summary: Dumpster fire is a harmless figure for chaos; its shadow is the cynicism that calls everything a disaster, and its image recalls Gehenna and the brand plucked out of the fire.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift in the phrase is toward cynicism. When every institution, year, and plan is labelled a dumpster fire, despair becomes a style and nothing seems worth repairing. A Christian can name a disaster honestly without surrendering to the mood; the Lord is still on His throne when the news is smoke. Scripture also traces many dumpster fires to a spark of the tongue, and the habit of mocking every failure is itself kindling.

The redemption is to remember both fires. One is the fire Jesus warned of in love, the real Gehenna, and the young should not be taught to laugh about it. The other is the fire from which He rescues: "a brand plucked out of the fire." Teach children that the Lord brings beauty from ashes, that a ruined project can be rebuilt and a ruined life restored, and that the right response to a dumpster fire is often a bucket of water and a prayer.
roots_summary: Dempster Brothers’ trademark Dumpster (1930s, Knoxville) + Old English fyr (fire) → 2000s figurative dumpster fire → 2016 ADS Word of the Year.
roots_lines: Old English fyr — fire
1930s: Dempster Brothers, Knoxville, Tennessee, the "Dempster Dumpster"
2000s: figurative dumpster fire; 2016: American Dialect Society Word of the Year
Biblical image: the valley of Hinnom, Gehenna, Jerusalem’s burning refuse and the name of hell
Biblical anchor: the fire is not quenched (Mar 9:44); a brand plucked out of the fire (Zec 3:2)
usage: "The group project was a dumpster fire."
How great a matter a little fire kindleth (Jas 3:5).
He gives beauty for ashes (Isa 61:3).

etymology: A truncated sentence ("I can’t even [deal with this / begin to express this]") used to signal emotion so overwhelming that words fail. It spread on Tumblr around 2011–2012 and became a Millennial catchphrase by 2013, often intensified as "I literally can’t even," "I can’t even right now," or simply "I can’t." It was used for joy (a cute puppy), outrage, and embarrassment alike, and was widely parodied as emblematic of Millennial speech.
biblical_def: I can’t even is the sentence that gives up halfway: the speaker is so overwhelmed, by delight, exasperation, or disbelief, that she cannot finish. It is usually comic, a performance of being speechless. The Christian observation: speechlessness has a real place in Scripture, and it is worth teaching what it is for. Some things are too great or too terrible for words. When Job’s friends saw his suffering, "they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great" (Job 2:13); that was their wisest moment. The Psalmist confesses, "I am so troubled that I cannot speak" (Psa 77:4). And the Holy Spirit Himself prays for believers who run out of words: "the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered" (Rom 8:26). The difference between that silence and the Millennial "I can’t even" is direction and proportion. The biblical silence is poured out before God ("pour out your heart before him," Psa 62:8); the catchphrase performs emotion for an audience, often about something small. Proverbs warns that "A fool uttereth all his mind" (Pro 29:11), and the constant display of overwhelm can become a kind of emotional self-indulgence. A father teaches his children to feel deeply, to be honest when words fail, and to take that wordless feeling to the Lord, who understands groans.
webster_summary: Millennial catchphrase (Tumblr, 2011–2013) for emotion too great for words; Scripture honours true speechlessness poured out before God (Rom 8:26; Psa 62:8) and cautions against performed overwhelm (Pro 29:11).
webster_full: I CAN’T EVEN, phr. (Millennial slang, c. 2011–present) Expresses being overwhelmed beyond words, comically or sincerely. Variants: "I literally can’t even," "I can’t."

Webster (1828), root even: EVEN, adverb e’vn. Noting a level or equality, or emphatically, a like manner or degree. As it has been done to you, even so shall it be done to others. Thou art a soldier even to Cato’s wishes, that is, your qualities, as a soldier, are equal to his wishes. 1. Noting equality or sameness of time; hence emphatically, the very time. I knew the facts, even when I wrote to you. 2. Noting, emphatically, identity of person. And behold I, even I, do bring a flood of waters on the earth. Genesis 6:17 . 3. Likewise; […]
Decode for parents: notice whether your child’s overwhelm is a joke, a performance, or a cry; the last kind needs you.
scriptures: Job 2:13
So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great.
Psa 77:4
Thou holdest mine eyes waking: I am so troubled that I cannot speak.
Rom 8:26
Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.
Psa 62:8
Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us. Selah.
A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards.
corruption_summary: I can’t even performs overwhelm for an audience, often over trifles; Scripture honours true wordlessness and directs it to God, who hears groanings that cannot be uttered.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is emotional inflation and display. The catchphrase makes being overwhelmed a constant public state, so that small things get the language of collapse and real collapse has no language left. It can also excuse a refusal to think: "I can’t even" ends a conversation that needed finishing. A generation trained to perform its feelings may find it hard to govern them.

The redemption is the honest silence turned toward God. The Psalms are full of men who could not finish their sentences and finished them in prayer; the Spirit carries what we cannot say. Teach the young to keep strong words for strong things, to sit silently with the grieving as Job’s friends did on their best days, and when they truly cannot even, to say so to their Father, who knows what they need before they ask.
roots_summary: Old English efne (even, level, "just") → intensifying even → truncated "I can’t even" (Tumblr, c. 2011) → 2013 catchphrase.
roots_lines: Old English efen / efne — level, equal; as adverb, "just," "indeed"
c. 2011–2012: "I can’t even" on Tumblr
2013: Millennial catchphrase; "I literally can’t even"
Widely parodied as emblematic Millennial speech
Biblical anchor: groanings which cannot be uttered (Rom 8:26); pour out your heart before him (Psa 62:8)
usage: "That puppy in a raincoat. I can’t even."
Job’s friends were wisest when they could not even speak (Job 2:13).
When you truly cannot, the Spirit maketh intercession (Rom 8:26).

etymology: From Latin litteralis (of letters), English since the fifteenth century for "according to the letter," "exactly." Its use as a mere intensifier, meaning the opposite ("I literally died"), is old: Dickens, Mark Twain, and F. Scott Fitzgerald all have examples. But Millennial speech made it constant ("I literally can’t," "it was literally the best"), and in 2011–2013 dictionaries, including Merriam-Webster and the Oxford dictionaries, noted the informal intensifying sense, to widespread protest. The word now carries two nearly opposite meanings.
biblical_def: In Millennial speech literally usually means "really, really" and often means "figuratively": "I literally died laughing." Nobody died. The word that once meant "exactly, according to the letter" has been worn into an intensifier that can say the opposite of what it says. The Christian observation: this is more than a pedant’s complaint, because Christians are people of a Book and of plain speech. God’s words mean what they say: "Every word of God is pure" (Pro 30:5); "The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times" (Psa 12:6). The Lord Jesus prayed, "Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth" (Joh 17:17). A people formed by a true Word ought to care that their own words are true. "Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour" (Eph 4:25). The intensifier literally is not usually a lie, since no one is deceived, but it is a symptom of speech that has lost its moorings: if literally can mean figuratively, the young lose a tool for saying "this really happened." That tool matters when you are telling someone that Jesus literally rose from the dead. "For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned" (Mat 12:37). A father teaches his children to say "really" when they mean really and "literally" when they mean it, and to keep one word strong enough to carry the resurrection.
webster_summary: An old adverb ("according to the letter") worn by Millennial overuse into an intensifier that can mean the opposite; a symptom of unmoored speech, whereas the Word of God is pure and true (Pro 30:5; Joh 17:17).
webster_full: LITERALLY, adv. (Millennial intensifying use, 2000s–present; older informal use since the 18th–19th c.) Used for emphasis, often of something not literally true: "I literally died." Standard sense: exactly, according to the letter.

Webster (1828), root literally: LITERALLY, adverb 1. According to the primary and natural import of words; not figuratively. A man and his wife cannot be literally one flesh. 2. With close adherence to words; word by word. So wild and ungovernable a poet cannot be translated literally
Decode for parents: keep one word in your family’s vocabulary strong enough to say "this really happened."
scriptures: Pro 30:5
Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him.
Psa 12:6
The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times.
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.
Eph 4:25
Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another.
For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned.
corruption_summary: Literally, worn into a mere intensifier, can now mean its opposite; the loss weakens a people of the Book who need words that say "this truly happened."
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is semantic decay with real costs. When the word for "actually, exactly" comes to mean "very" or even "not actually," speech loses its ability to mark fact from figure. That matters most for the gospel, which is not a mood but a report of events: "that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day" (1Co 15:3-4). A generation that hears "literally" as hype hears the creed as hype too.

The recovery is careful speech, practised in small things. Christians should be known for meaning what they say, for saying what happened, and for using big words for big things. Teach children the difference between a figure of speech, which Scripture uses gloriously, and an exaggeration that blurs truth. Then, when they say Jesus literally rose, it will carry the weight of the word.
roots_summary: Latin littera (letter) → litteralis → English literal, literally (15th c., "exactly") → 18th–19th-c. intensifier → Millennial ubiquity → 2011–2013 dictionary recognition.
roots_lines: Latin littera — a letter of the alphabet; litteralis — of letters
15th c.: literally — according to the letter, exactly
18th–19th c.: informal intensifier (Dickens, Twain); 20th c.: Fitzgerald
2011–2013: dictionaries note the intensifying sense; public protest
Biblical anchor: every word of God is pure (Pro 30:5); thy word is truth (Joh 17:17)
usage: "I literally died when he walked in."
Keep one word strong enough for the resurrection (1Co 15:4).
By thy words thou shalt be justified (Mat 12:37).
